q-1886.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{3}$ if $f(x)=@a@\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}.$
q-1886.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(@a@\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(@a@\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+{x}^{-1}) \\  & =@a@(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-@a@\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\sqrt{3}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) & =-@a@\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\sqrt{3})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =-@a@\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\sqrt{3})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-1905.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ if $f(x)=@a@x-\sqrt{2}sec⁡x.$
q-1905.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(@a@x-\sqrt{2}sec⁡x) \\  & =@a@-\sqrt{2}sec⁡xtan⁡x\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =@a@-\sqrt{2}sec⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})tan⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =@a@-\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2})(1) \\  & =@a@-2 \\  & =@correct@.\end{aligned}
$$

q-104437.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ if $f(x)=@factor@x\operatorname{cot}x.$
q-104437.:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the derivative using the product rule:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(@factor@x\operatorname{cot}x) \\  & =@factor@\operatorname{cot}x+@factor@x(-{csc}^{2}x) \\  & =@factor@\operatorname{cot}x-@factor@x{csc}^{2}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ in the derivative and get

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{\pi /4} & =@factor@\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{4})-@factor@\frac{\pi }{4}{csc}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =@a@-@factor@\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot (\sqrt{2})^{2} \\  & =@a@-@halfpi@.\end{aligned}
$$

q-340642.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the product rule and sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(@factor@\operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x) \\  & =(-@factor@\operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x)(\operatorname{cot}x)+(@factor@\operatorname{csc}x)(-{csc}^{2}x) \\  & =-@factor@\operatorname{csc}x({cot}^{2}x+{csc}^{2}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and evaluate the slope $m:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={g}^{'}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-@factor@\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})[{cot}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{2})+{csc}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =-@a@\cdot ({0}^{2}+{1}^{2}) \\  & =-@a@\end{aligned}
$$

q-104442.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ if $f(x)=\frac{sec⁡x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{@a@{x}^{2}}{\pi }.$
q-104442.:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the derivative of each term and then add them, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{sec⁡x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{@a@{x}^{2}}{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{sec⁡xtan⁡x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{@twice@x}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ in the derivative and get

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{\pi /3} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot sec⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot tan⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{@twice@}{\pi }\cdot \frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{3}+@qpart@ \\  & =2+@qpart@ \\  & =@correct@.\end{aligned}
$$

q-1904.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ if $f(x)=-{x}^{2}+@a@csc⁡x.$
q-1904.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{d}{dx}(-{x}^{2}+@a@csc⁡x) \\  & =2\cdot (-x)+@a@(-csc⁡xcot⁡x) \\  & =-2x-@a@csc⁡xcot⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the derivative and get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =-2(\frac{\pi }{6})-@a@csc⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})cot⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}-@a@\cdot 2\cdot \sqrt{3} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}-@twice@\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-340630.:question/worked-solution:

$$

$$

Now, we substitute $x=\pi $ and evaluate the slope $m:$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={h}^{′}(\pi ) & =@factor@{e}^{\pi }+3\operatorname{sec}⁡(\pi )\operatorname{tan}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =@factor@{e}^{\pi }+3\cdot (-1)\cdot 0 \\  & =@factor@{e}^{\pi }\end{aligned}

q-340660.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{@a@x}{sec⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(@a@x)\cdot sec⁡x-@a@x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(sec⁡x)}{{sec}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{@a@sec⁡x-@a@x\cdot sec⁡xtan⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{@a@sec⁡x(1-xtan⁡x)}{{sec}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{@a@(1-xtan⁡x)}{sec⁡x}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=0$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =\frac{@a@(1-0\cdot tan⁡0)}{sec⁡0} \\  & =\frac{@a@(1-0)}{1} \\  & =@a@\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-70874.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ if $f(x)=ln⁡x+@a@csc⁡x.$
q-70874.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(ln⁡x+@a@csc⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}+@a@(-csc⁡xcot⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}-@a@csc⁡xcot⁡x\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{3})}-@a@csc⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})cot⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }-@a@(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }-@a@(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\pi }-@qpart@.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical-quotient.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ if $f(x) = \dfrac{-2\cot x}{\sin x}.$
canonical-quotient.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{-2cot⁡x}{sin⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2cot⁡x)\cdot sin⁡x-(-2cot⁡x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(sin⁡x)}{{[sin⁡x]}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-2(-{csc}^{2}⁡x)\cdot sin⁡x+2cot⁡x\cdot (cos⁡x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{2csc⁡x+2cot⁡xcos⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{2csc⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+2cot⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})cos⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})}{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (\sqrt{2})+2\cdot (1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
